h1:
Ban Mai Century Market Food Crawl
+ Bang Pakong Riverside Eats
intro: Chachoengsao sits just over an hour from Bangkok, but it feels like a different city — especially Ban Mai Market, a row of wooden shophouses along the Bang Pakong River still selling the same old-school snacks your grandparents grew up on. We've turned it into a real 2-day eat-and-walk plan so you can hit both the market stalls and the riverside dinner spots in one trip.

blocks.html: Ban Mai Market is a double-storey wooden shophouse market on the banks of the Bang Pakong River, dating back to the reign of King Rama V. You can walk straight through end to end, with the best food scattered in different corners — savoury dishes, sweets, old-school coffee, and produce straight from local orchards. The thing many people miss: the market is only fully open on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays (roughly 8am–5pm). On weekdays a few stalls open, but not the full lineup. If you're coming to eat properly, aim for a weekend.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: Ban Mai Market is busiest from late morning to early afternoon, and several popular stalls sell out before 3pm. Try to arrive before 11am so you can try everything. Parking inside the market is limited too — on weekends, go early or park at Wat Sothon and continue to the market by local transport.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Eat your way through Ban Mai Market + pay respects at Wat Sothon

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Century market + Wat Sothon + riverside dinner

items.note: It's about a 1 hr 15 min drive from Bangkok, or take the Eastern Line train to Chachoengsao station and continue from there. Leave early and you'll reach the market while every stall is still open.

items.activity: Arrive at Ban Mai Market, start eating from the entrance
items.note: Begin with savoury dishes while you're still hungry — pak mor steamed noodles, hor jor rolls, pork-and-plum soup — then work your way toward the fried and grilled stalls.

items.activity: Stop for old-school coffee, rest your legs
items.note: Pae Ia coffee shop is a long-running spot in the market — sip traditional sock-brewed coffee in a wooden shophouse setting, with photogenic corners everywhere.

items.activity: Hunt down old-style sweets + grab souvenirs
items.note: Charcoal-oven egg cakes, fresh khanom pia pastries, traditional sweets on skewers, and fruit shipped straight from Chachoengsao orchards. The stalls with long queues are usually a safe bet.

items.activity: Take a riverside break in the market, watch the Bang Pakong roll by
items.note: Several stalls have seating facing the river — order some snacks, sit in the breeze, then go back to cover the corners you missed.

items.activity: Drive over to pay respects to Luang Pho Phuttha Sothon at Wat Sothon Wararam Worawihan
items.note: Just a few kilometres from the market, this is Chachoengsao's most revered temple, open Sat–Sun roughly 6:30am–5pm. Make your wishes, then stroll along the riverfront in front of the temple.

items.activity: Check into your hotel in town, drop your bags, rest up
items.note: Central Chachoengsao has hotels and riverside stays to choose from, with easy access to dinner spots.

items.activity: Dinner at a Bang Pakong riverside restaurant
items.note: Book a riverside table ahead on weekends. Order grilled river prawns and sea bass, and catch the cool evening breeze by the water to close out the day.

blocks.html: Day one is about covering the market thoroughly and visiting the town's signature temple. If you arrive early and walk quickly, you might have time to squeeze in a riverside café before checking in — no need to rush yourself ragged. The fun of the century-old market is being able to wander at your own pace.

blocks.text: Food at Ban Mai Market you shouldn't miss

items.name: Pak mor steamed noodles
items.blurb: Thin steamed rice sheets wrapped around minced pork, topped with fried-garlic sauce. It's a Phanom Sarakham specialty you can find right here in the market — light enough to start a meal, and best eaten while it's still hot.

items.name: Hor jor rolls + pork-and-plum soup
items.blurb: Crispy-outside, soft-inside hor jor rolls are a staple of old Chinese markets, while the clear pork-and-plum soup is mellow with a gentle sourness — old-school dishes the market stalls have passed down for generations.

items.name: Egg-wrapped pad thai with river prawns
items.blurb: Pad thai folded in a thin egg wrap — some stalls use butterfly-pea egg for a striking blue colour — loaded with big river prawns from the Bang Pakong. A photogenic plate with bold flavour that earns its price.

items.name: Charcoal-oven egg cakes
items.blurb: Old-style egg cakes baked over charcoal, with a faint smoky aroma, crisp outside and soft inside. Made fresh and sold by the tray — far better eaten warm at the stall than taken home.

items.name: Old-school coffee at Pae Ia
items.blurb: A long-running coffee shop in the market, brewing traditional sock-filtered coffee. The wooden shophouse setting feels like time stopped — a good spot to rest your legs mid-crawl.

items.name: Fresh khanom pia pastries
items.blurb: Soft-crust pastries with a generous filling, made fresh in the market. Buy a few to snack on or carry home as a gift — several fillings to choose from, at friendly prices.

items.name: Fruit + orchard souvenirs
items.blurb: Chachoengsao is known for mangoes and seasonal fruit, much of it brought straight from the orchards — fresher and cheaper than what you'd buy in Bangkok. A great way to wrap up the trip is loading up on souvenirs.

blocks.title: Eat smart, don't fill up too fast
blocks.html: The market is longer than it looks. Buy small portions and share within your group so you can try more stalls without getting stuffed. Start with the salty savoury dishes, then finish with sweets and coffee.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Riverside café + last great stalls before heading home

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: An easy riverside morning, then back to Bangkok

items.note: Rice porridge or coffee at a spot in town — save room for a bigger meal later in the morning. No rush; today is the chill day.

items.activity: Settle into a café on the Bang Pakong River
items.note: Chachoengsao has plenty of riverside cafés, some renovated from old wooden houses, with bakeries and river views. Great for photos and a long sit.

items.activity: Lunch at a riverside restaurant you haven't tried
items.note: If you went to Ekkanek on day one, try Ruen Rom Sai or Mathurot Ruen Phae today for a change of scenery on the floating raft section.

items.activity: Swing back to Ban Mai Market for souvenirs you missed
items.note: If it's still a weekend and the market is open, drop by to grab the sweets and fruit you noted down before you head off.
Avoid leaving on a Sunday evening when traffic builds up. Heading out around 3pm gets you home before it's too late.

blocks.html: If you only have a single day, just drop Day 2 and condense the main activities from Day 1 (market + Wat Sothon + riverside dinner) into one day — it makes a perfectly satisfying round-trip food trip from Bangkok.

blocks.text: Bang Pakong riverside restaurants for dinner

blocks.html: Chachoengsao's charm is being a town right on the Bang Pakong River, and come evening the riverside restaurants take centre stage — cool breeze, water views, and big river prawns. These are the spots locals and reviews bring up most often; pick one to book that fits your plan.

items.name: Ekkanek
items.blurb: A well-known Thai seafood restaurant in town. Crowd favourites are the big grilled river prawns and crispy lemongrass sea bass. Relaxed atmosphere, great for groups.

items.name: Ruen Rom Sai
items.blurb: A Bang Pakong riverside restaurant with a Thai Select award, offering an air-conditioned zone, an outdoor zone, and a floating raft section over the water — take your pick. Good for a long, leisurely dinner.

items.name: Mathurot Ruen Phae
items.blurb: A restaurant on a floating raft over the river, so you're genuinely sitting above the water with a classic river-town feel. Best for people who care more about atmosphere than flash.

items.name: Kin Lom Chom Pla 8 Riu
items.blurb: A much-reviewed riverside spot serving seafood and Thai dishes, with open river views. Good for photos and catching the breeze at sunset.

blocks.title: On reservations
blocks.html: At the popular riverside restaurants, the waterfront tables fill up fast on weekends. Call ahead and specifically ask for a riverside or raft table. Without a booking you may end up in the inner zone, where the view just isn't the same.

blocks.text: How to get there and plan it right

items: From Bangkok — about a 1 hr 15 min drive via the motorway, or take the Eastern Line train to Chachoengsao station and continue to the market by songthaew or taxi.
Best days to go — Saturdays, Sundays or public holidays, when the market is fully open. On weekdays a few stalls open but not the full lineup.
Timing — arrive before 11am to try everything; several popular stalls sell out before 3pm.
Parking — limited inside the market. On weekends, go early, or park near Wat Sothon and continue to the market by local transport.
Budget — eating your way through the market runs about ฿200–400 per person; riverside dinner runs about ฿300–600 per person, depending on whether you order river prawns.

faq.q: What days is Ban Mai Market open?
faq.a: It's only fully open on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays, roughly 8am–5pm. On weekdays a few stalls open but not the full lineup. If you want plenty of variety, come on a weekend and arrive before noon so you can try everything before stalls sell out.

faq.q: What food at Ban Mai Market should I try?
faq.a: The ones people mention most are pak mor steamed noodles, hor jor rolls, pork-and-plum soup, egg-wrapped pad thai with river prawns, charcoal-oven egg cakes, fresh khanom pia pastries, and old-school coffee in the wooden shophouses — finished off with fruit and souvenirs from Chachoengsao orchards.

faq.q: Is Ban Mai Market far from Bangkok?
faq.a: Not far — about a 1 hr 15 min drive from Bangkok, or take the Eastern Line train to Chachoengsao station and continue to the market from there. It's an easy round-trip day, or stay one night to catch the riverside restaurants in the evening and a café the next morning.

faq.q: Which Bang Pakong riverside restaurant is best for dinner?
faq.a: Spots locals and reviews bring up often include Ekkanek (seafood, grilled river prawns), Ruen Rom Sai (with a floating raft section, Thai Select), Mathurot Ruen Phae, and Kin Lom Chom Pla 8 Riu. Call ahead to book a riverside table on weekends.

faq.q: How much does a Ban Mai Market trip cost?
faq.a: Eating your way through the market runs about 200–400 THB per person, enough to fill up and try a good range. Add a riverside dinner and it's roughly another 300–600 THB per person, depending on whether you order river prawns or larger seafood.
